angle: color each level with three matching colors instead of one, so the one-third falls out by symmetry with no algebra; then the same trick gives 1/8 for nine pieces and asks viewers for sixteen
title: Keep adding quarters forever and you get exactly 1/3
description:
A quarter, plus a quarter of a quarter, plus a quarter of that, forever: 1/4 + 1/16 + 1/64 + ... adds up to exactly 1/3. Split a square into four, color three corners with three different colors, and split the fourth corner again. The three colors always match, so each one ends up with exactly a third of the square.

After 5 steps the total is 341/1024 = 0.333. The same trick with nine pieces gives 1/9 + 1/81 + ... = 1/8. Checked with exact fractions and by throwing 300,000 random points into the picture.
facts_checked: partial sums stay below 1/3 (gap after k terms = (1/3)(1/4)^k), never reach 1/2
each level: three equal squares plus one to split, so each color takes 1/3
Monte Carlo: 300,000 random points, share landing on amber = 0.3337
source: https://mathworld.wolfram.com/GeometricSeries.html (standard geometric series a/(1-r)); Wikipedia '1/4 + 1/16 + 1/64 + 1/256 + ⋯' (not fetched today: blocked by network policy)

beats.say: Take a quarter, plus a quarter of that, forever. You get exactly one third.
That feels wrong. Quarters add up to halves, or to one. Where would a third come from?
Start with one square. Cut it into four. One corner is a quarter.
Color three of the corners, each a different color. Leave the fourth one empty.
Cut that empty corner into four, and do the same. Then again. And again.
At every size, the three colors get the same amount. None of them is ever ahead.
The squares fill everything, so each color covers exactly one third of the square.
And the amber squares are a quarter, a sixteenth, a sixty-fourth, and so on. That's our sum.
After just 5 steps, the total is 0.333. It creeps up on one third and never passes it.
Cut into nine instead, and the same trick gives one eighth. What do you get with sixteen?
